clues.title: Stop sign: bus stop sign
text: Finland has two styles of bus stop signs, a blue and white one, and a yellow and black one.
NOTE: This can be used to tell Finland apart from Sweden, which has many different bus stop signs, most of which have the names of the stops on them.

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines
text: Where present, outer road lines will always be solid white lines.
**NOTE:** Unlike Sweden and Norway, Finland does not use dashed outside lines. The only exception to this are the Åland Islands in southwest Finland, which do use dashes.

clues.title: Pole: Snow Poles
text: In Finland, it is common to find orange snow poles with a thin white band near the top.
These are also found commonly in Norway and Sweden, but with a much wider white band, lower down on the pole.
They can also have multiple white bands, while Finnish snow poles usually have just one band.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Google car: Gen 3 Autumn
text: A lot of Generation 3 coverage was taken in autumn, meaning that trees in this coverage often have distinct fall colours.
This is significantly less common in Generation 3 coverage in the other Nordics.
This means that when you are faced with a tough decision between countries, a fall vibe can be a good clue for Finland.

clues.title: Sign: Yellow Sign Border
text: On traffic signs that have a red border, you will find a thin yellow stroke on the edge of the sign.
You will not see this in any other Nordic country.

clues.title: Google car: Shitcam
text: Google used a weird, low-quality camera in Finland.
This camera is known as the official Ari (or “Shitcam”).
It has a wide circular car blur, and can be distinguished from Generation 2 by its lack of a sky halo and often somewhat brownish colours.
Within Europe, Finland is the only country that has coverage with this camera.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Bollard: Bollards
text: Finland has long black-and-white bollards with a rectangular, white reflector on the front and two dots on the back.
They can be either round or thin and curved.
The black strip is typically diagonal.
They can look somewhat similar to bollards found in other Northern European countries.

clues.title: Language: Finnish
text: Finnish is a Finnic language closely related to Estonian. It is completely unrelated to all other major Nordic languages. The Finnish alphabet includes the letters **Ä** and **Ö**. While these are also used in Swedish, Finnish can be told apart from it by the many long words and especially the double vowels, which are rare in Swedish.
Estonian, to which Finnish is closely related, uses the letters **Õ** and **Ü** plus the same **Ä** and **Ö** as in Finnish.
The Finnish word for road is **tie**. This is unlike Estonian which uses **tee** instead.
The Finnish word for street is **katu**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Street sign: Swedish
text: In some coastal areas of southern and western Finland, you will find bilingual signs in Finnish and Swedish. Street signs in these regions typically include both **-tie** and **-vägen** (meaning road) or both **-katu** and **-gatan** (meaning street).
NOTE: Swedish is also spoken monolingually on the Åland Islands (and in Sweden, of course).
